newsitem.title: USA: U.S. regulators seek broader power market role.
newsitem.headline: U.S. regulators seek broader power market role.

text.p: Federal energy regulators Thursday advised Congress to make states open their power markets to competition, but allow them to opt out if they can prove that customer choice would do more harm than good.
"Congress should legislate a national policy to promote competition in retail markets," said Elizabeth Moler, chairwoman of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission.

"I recommend that you direct that the states establish consumer choice programs, but with the opportunity to opt out if a state determines that retail competition is contrary to its own needs and interests," she said.
Moler spoke at the third in a string of workshops held by the Senate Energy Committee on whether Congress should require all states to give consumers a choice of power suppliers.
Most of the state utility commissions represented asked Congress not to interfere with states already promoting customer choice nor spur slower states into action.

"Congressional action should ... focus on assisting the states," and "promote development of robust competition in regional markets," said Vermont Public Service Board chairman Richard Cowart, adding that federal legislation should clarify the authority of FERC versus state commissions.
Except for Pennsylvania commissioner John Quain, none asked Congress to set a deadline for opening power markets.
Moler said, deadline or no deadline, Congress should first expand the FERC's authority to order open access on the 30 percent of transmission lines that now fall outside its realm.

The commission has already required all investor-owned utilities to open their wires to competing power producers. To level the wholesale power market, Moler said government-owned utilities and co-ops should also have to open their wires.
Moler also urged Congress to give the FERC authority to punish those who violate standards set by the North American Electric Reliability Council to ensure steady power supplies.
"Reliability in a competitive environment is too important to be left to a voluntary regime," she said.
FERC should also have authority to address conflicting requirements imposed on utilities operating in several different states, and to require reciprocal service she said.
Federal legislation should address tax laws that limit government-owned utilities which issue tax-exempt bonds from offering transmission service to private power suppliers.

It should also make clear that states have the authority to allow utilities to recover the costs of investments that were made to serve customers who they might now lose as other power suppliers enter the market.
